title: The Last Transmission
content:
At 02:17 on the morning of June 14, 2189, the observatory on Europa received a transmission that should not have existed.

Dr. Mara Voss had been monitoring the outer system for six hours when the signal appeared on her console. It was faint at first, almost indistinguishable from the electromagnetic interference produced by Jupiter's magnetosphere.

She adjusted the receiver.

The signal became clearer.

Then a sequence of numbers appeared on the screen.

Mara stared at them.

— That's impossible.

Her colleague, Elias Chen, looked up from his station.

— What is it?

— I don't know yet.

She began analyzing the transmission.

It was repeating every eleven seconds.

Not random noise.

Not a natural phenomenon.

A message.

Elias walked toward her.

— Could it be an automated probe?

— It could.

— A human transmission?

— No.

— How can you be sure?

Mara pointed at the screen.

— Because we're receiving it from beyond Neptune.

Elias frowned.

— That's not possible. Nothing we've launched is that far away.

— Exactly.

They continued listening.

The signal contained no recognizable language. Instead, it consisted of mathematical sequences arranged in increasingly complex patterns.

Mara began translating them.

Prime numbers.

Geometric relationships.

Physical constants.

Then something unexpected appeared.

A timestamp.

JUNE 14, 2189 — 02:17

Elias stared at it.

— That's now.

Mara nodded.

— I know.

Another sequence appeared.

Then another.

Mara's hands became cold.

— It's describing us.

— What?

— Our observatory. Our equipment. Even the number of people in this room.

Elias looked around.

There were only three researchers present.

— It knows we're here.

Mara continued decoding.

A final sentence emerged.

YOU WILL BE LISTENING.

She leaned back.

— It knew we would receive the message.

Elias looked at the clock.

— When was it sent?

Mara checked the transmission data.

Her expression changed.

— That's the problem.

— What?

— The signal was transmitted from Europa.

Elias looked at the enormous planet visible through the observation window.

— That's impossible.

— I know.

He examined the data.

— Europa is only a few minutes away by communication relay.

— Not this signal.

Mara pointed toward the screen.

— Look at the timestamp of transmission.

Elias read it.

His face became pale.

— Tomorrow.

By morning, the entire observatory had been placed under restricted access.

The transmission continued.

Every eleven seconds.

Scientists from Earth joined the investigation remotely, but no one could explain how the signal had been generated.

The source appeared to be Europa.

But the message contained information about events that had not happened yet.

At 10:00, the transmission predicted a power fluctuation.

At 10:03, it happened.

At 11:27, it predicted that a communications satellite would fail.

At 11:27, the satellite stopped responding.

By noon, nobody believed the predictions were coincidences.

Mara stood before the central display.

— What happens next?

The system displayed another sequence.

She translated it.

AT 18:40, YOU WILL OPEN THE GATE.

Elias frowned.

— What gate?

Mara shook her head.

— I don't know.

They searched the observatory's systems.

There was no gate.

No physical structure.

No security protocol with that name.

Then Mara remembered something.

— The Europa excavation project.

Elias turned toward her.

— The abandoned station?

— Yes.

Twenty years earlier, scientists had discovered an unusual structure beneath Europa's ice.

It had been sealed after several unexplained equipment failures.

The official explanation had been geological instability.

Mara had never believed it.

— You're thinking about the artifact.

— I'm thinking about what they found underneath the ice.

Elias stared at her.

— You think the transmission is coming from there?

— I think it might be.

At 18:37, the observatory's main systems began malfunctioning.

Lights flickered.

Displays went dark.

Then the entire station became silent.

Mara looked at the central screen.

A single message appeared.

YOU WILL BE OPENING THE GATE.

Elias whispered:

— We haven't done anything.

A deep vibration passed through the station.

Then the floor moved.

The researchers rushed toward the observation chamber.

Europa's surface was changing.

A long fracture had appeared across the ice.

It extended for kilometers.

Something beneath the surface was rising.

Mara stared through the reinforced glass.

— My God.

Elias stepped beside her.

— What is that?

A structure emerged from the ice.

It was enormous.

Smooth black walls reflected the distant sunlight.

No machinery was visible.

No doors.

No windows.

Yet something about it looked unmistakably artificial.

The transmission continued.

THE GATE WILL BE OPEN.

Then the structure began to unfold.

Sections of its surface moved silently apart.

A circular opening appeared.

Beyond it was darkness.

Mara's console suddenly activated.

A message appeared.

YOU HAVE BEEN WAITING FOR US.

She whispered:

— We haven't.

The answer appeared immediately.

YOU WILL BE.

The structure remained open for several minutes.

Then a beam of light emerged from its center.

It crossed the ice and disappeared into space.

The observatory detected it immediately.

Elias checked the trajectory.

— It's pointing toward Earth.

Mara's expression tightened.

— Is it a weapon?

— I don't think so.

— Then what is it?

He examined the data.

— A transmission.

Mara stared at him.

— Another message?

— No.

He looked up.

— A map.

The display filled with coordinates.

Thousands of them.

Stars.

Planets.

Galaxies.

Then one final coordinate appeared.

It was not in their galaxy.

Mara understood.

— They're showing us where they came from.

Elias looked at the distance.

— That's impossible.

— Apparently, we've been saying that a lot today.

The transmission stopped.

For the first time in almost twenty hours, the observatory was completely silent.

Then a final message appeared.

WE WILL BE ARRIVING.

Mara stared at the words.

— When?

The system provided no date.

Only another sequence.

Elias began calculating.

His expression gradually changed.

— What?

He looked at her.

— I think I know.

— How long?

He hesitated.

— Three hundred and twelve years.

Mara looked toward Europa.

— Then we'll never see them.

Elias shook his head.

— No.

He pointed toward the transmission data.

— The message wasn't sent for us.

Mara frowned.

— What do you mean?

— It was sent for whoever will be here when they arrive.

She stared at the screen.

The meaning slowly became clear.

Humanity had not been invited to witness their arrival.

It had been warned.

Three centuries later, historians would describe June 14, 2189, as the moment humanity stopped considering itself alone in the universe.

By then, Mara and Elias would have been long gone.

The observatory would have become a museum.

Europa would have been transformed into a research colony.

And generations of scientists would have been studying the mysterious structure beneath the ice.

They would still be searching for answers.

But they would also be waiting.

Somewhere beyond the stars, another civilization would be traveling toward them.

Humanity would be watching.

Scientists would be monitoring the skies.

Spacecraft would be patrolling the outer system.

And somewhere, perhaps millions of kilometers away, an unknown vessel would be approaching.

They would not know what the visitors would want.

They would not know whether they would come as explorers, conquerors, or something entirely beyond those categories.

But they would know one thing.

The future would not be empty.

Humanity would be living beneath a sky filled with possibilities.

And one day, while the descendants of those who had first received the transmission would be watching the stars, the last message would finally make sense.

YOU WILL BE LISTENING.

They had been.

They would still be listening.

And soon, they would be answering.
